George Eldon Ladd, The Blessed Hope

Ladd, of Fuller Theological Seminary, argued that the New Testament knows one coming of Christ after the tribulation. He linked this to a historic premillennialism free of dispensational distinctives. Walvoord replied in The Rapture Question (1957), and the exchange shaped the modern debate.
J. Oliver Buswell and the mid-tribulation view

J. Oliver Buswell, former president of Wheaton College, set out a mid-tribulation rapture at the seventh trumpet in his Systematic Theology (1962-63), following Norman Harrison (1941). Harold Ockenga is sometimes linked with this middle ground, though by 1955 he publicly argued that the church would go through the tribulation.
Robert Gundry, The Church and the Tribulation

Robert Gundry gave a detailed exegetical defence of posttribulationism, especially on the Greek of 1 Thessalonians 4 and Revelation 3:10. Pretribulationists such as Walvoord and Ryrie wrote critical replies.
Three Views on the Rapture (first edition)

Edited by Richard Reiter, this book set out pre-tribulation (Paul Feinberg), mid-tribulation (Gleason Archer) and post-tribulation (Douglas Moo) views, each with responses. It became a standard textbook for the debate.
Marvin Rosenthal, The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church

Rosenthal, formerly with a pretribulational mission to the Jewish people, argued that the church is raptured after the cosmic signs and before the day of the Lord's wrath. The book introduced the prewrath view to a wide audience.
Robert Van Kampen, The Sign

Businessman and collector Robert Van Kampen, who had shaped Rosenthal's thinking, set out the prewrath system in full, with charts of Daniel's seventieth week. He followed it with The Rapture Question Answered (1997).
Left Behind

Tim LaHaye and Jerry B. Jenkins began a novel series about people left on earth after a pre-tribulation rapture. The books sold tens of millions of copies and made the view widely known in popular culture, though many scholars, including some pretribulationists, questioned their use of fiction for doctrine.
Three Views on the Rapture (second edition)

Edited by Alan Hultberg, the new edition replaced the mid-tribulation view with prewrath. Craig Blaising argued for pre-tribulation, Hultberg for prewrath and Douglas Moo for post-tribulation. The change reflected the decline of midtribulationism and the rise of prewrath.

Amillennialists hold that the thousand years of Revelation 20 is the present age between Christ's first and second comings. Christ reigns now from heaven, and departed believers reign with him. The age ends with one visible return of Christ, one general resurrection and judgment, and the new heavens and new earth. Many prefer the name 'realized millennialism', since they do believe in a millennium, one that is happening now.

Revelation 20 begins a new vision that goes back to the start of the church age, as chapters 12 and 17 also do. It does not follow chapter 19 in time. The battle of 20:7-10 is the same final battle as 16:14-16 and 19:17-21, seen again from another angle. Both draw on Ezekiel 38-39.

Satan was bound at Christ's first coming, when Jesus 'bound the strong man' (Matthew 12:29) and cast out the ruler of this world (John 12:31). The binding has one stated purpose: he can no longer deceive the nations. He cannot stop the gospel going to all peoples, or gather the world against the church, until he is released at the end.

The first resurrection is spiritual, not bodily. Most amillennialists read it as the believer's soul entering Christ's presence at death to reign with him, since John sees 'souls' (Revelation 20:4). Others read it as the new birth (John 5:24-25). The bodily resurrection of all people comes once, at the end.

Symbolic. Revelation uses numbers as symbols, and a thousand is ten times ten times ten, a picture of completeness. It stands for the full period God has set between the two comings of Christ, however long that is.
Present age: Christ reigns from heaven and Satan is bound (the millennium now)
The gospel goes to all nations while good and evil grow together
Satan released for a short time; final rebellion against the church
One general resurrection of the just and the unjust

Amillennialists expect the gospel to spread to every nation through the whole age, and the church to grow. They also expect evil to ripen alongside it, like wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). Many expect a short time of severe persecution at the very end, when Satan is released. So the line is roughly level: real kingdom growth, but no golden age before the return.

It fits the New Testament's simple pattern of two ages divided by one return, with one resurrection and one judgment (John 5:28-29; Matthew 25:31-46). It reads Revelation's numbers and images in a consistent symbolic way. It has had wide support in church history since Augustine, including most Reformation confessions.

Critics say a Satan locked and sealed in a pit fits poorly with a Satan who prowls now (1 Peter 5:8) and blinds unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4). They also argue that 'came to life' in Revelation 20:4-5 must mean the same both times, so a spiritual first and bodily second resurrection is inconsistent. Amillennialists reply that the binding is limited to one purpose, and that John deliberately contrasts two kinds of life.

Postmillennialists hold that Christ returns after the millennium. Through the preaching of the gospel and the work of the Holy Spirit, most of the world's peoples will be converted. Christ's reign from heaven will bring a long age of righteousness and peace on earth. Christ then returns for one general resurrection and judgment.

Many postmillennialists, like amillennialists, read Revelation 20 as the present age from Christ's ascension (Warfield, Gentry). Others read it as a later, golden stage of the church age, after the gospel has overcome the beast (many Puritans, Jonathan Edwards). Either way the reign is Christ's heavenly rule, worked out through the church on earth.

Satan was bound by Christ's death, resurrection and ascension (Matthew 12:29; Colossians 2:15). Because he can no longer deceive the nations, the gospel will progressively win them over the course of the age. The strong man is bound, so his house is being plundered, nation by nation.

Spiritual. Most postmillennialists read it as regeneration and union with the risen Christ, who has raised believers and seated them with him (Ephesians 2:5-6; John 5:24-25). Warfield read it as the souls of believers reigning with Christ in heaven. The bodily resurrection of all comes at Christ's one return.

Usually symbolic: a long and complete period, probably far longer than a thousand literal years. Gentry compares God owning 'the cattle on a thousand hills' (Psalms 50:10), where the number means 'all'. Some older postmillennialists expected a literal thousand years of gospel triumph at the end of the church age.
Christ enthroned at his resurrection and ascension
Gospel age: the Great Commission advances among the nations
Conversion of most nations, including a large turning of the Jewish people; a long era of peace
Brief final rebellion
General resurrection and final judgment

Postmillennialists expect the gospel to grow like the mustard seed and the leaven until it fills the world (Matthew 13:31-33). The growth is gradual and uneven, with real setbacks along the way. It comes through preaching, prayer and the Spirit, not by force or politics. Most expect a brief rebellion just before the end, so the rise is not perfectly smooth.

It takes seriously the many promises that all nations will worship God, and that Christ must reign until every enemy is under his feet. It gives strong motivation for mission and for faithfulness in every area of life. It was widely held among the Puritans and the leaders of the modern missionary movement, as Iain Murray has shown.

Critics point to texts that seem to expect persecution, apostasy and lawlessness until the end (Matthew 24:12; Luke 18:8; 2 Timothy 3:1-5). The world wars of the twentieth century weakened the view's appeal. Postmillennialists answer that some of these texts concern the first century, others a brief final rebellion, and that the gospel has in fact spread dramatically across the world.

Historic premillennialists hold that Christ will return before a future thousand-year reign on earth. The church passes through the final tribulation and is gathered at Christ's single visible return. Believers are raised at his coming and reign with him over the nations; the rest of the dead are raised after the thousand years. It is called 'historic' because forms of it were held by Papias, Justin and Irenaeus, and it does not depend on a dispensational distinction between Israel and the church.

Revelation 20 follows chapter 19 in time: Christ's return (19:11-21) is followed by the binding of Satan and the reign of the saints. The beast and the false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire in 19:20, and Satan joins them there later (20:10). Ladd argues that the visions read most naturally as one continuous story.

Satan's binding is future. It begins at Christ's return and is far more complete than any present restraint: he is thrown into the abyss, shut in and sealed, so he cannot deceive the nations at all. Historic premillennialists grant that Satan was defeated at the cross, but say Revelation 20 describes a further stage of that defeat.

A bodily resurrection of believers at Christ's return (1 Corinthians 15:23; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). The same verb 'came to life' is used for 'the rest of the dead' in 20:5, which nearly all agree is bodily. Henry Alford famously argued that if one is spiritual and the other bodily in the same passage, language loses its meaning.

Many historic premillennialists say the number may be a symbol for a long era, while insisting the era itself is real, earthly and future. Others take it literally. What matters to them is that a real kingdom on earth comes between Christ's return and the eternal state.
Church age: the gospel goes to all nations
Great tribulation and the Antichrist; the church suffers but endures
Return of Christ; believers raised and caught up to meet him
Christ and his saints reign over the earth for a thousand years
Satan released; final rebellion crushed
Resurrection of the rest of the dead and final judgment

Historic premillennialists expect the gospel to bear real fruit in every nation through the age (Matthew 24:14). They do not expect the church to fail. But they read the New Testament as expecting a final time of great tribulation and falling away before the return. The kingdom's full, open triumph comes only when Christ himself returns.

It reads Revelation 19-20 in its most natural order and takes 'came to life' the same way both times. It has strong support in the second-century church. It explains texts that link Christ's coming with his visible rule over the nations, without needing a pretribulation rapture or a sharp Israel-church distinction.

Critics ask why no New Testament text outside Revelation 20 clearly mentions an earthly kingdom between the return and the end, while many link one resurrection and judgment to the return (John 5:28-29; Matthew 25:31-46). They also ask who the mortal nations in the millennium are. Premillennialists answer that later revelation can clarify earlier texts, and that survivors of the nations enter the kingdom.

Dispensational premillennialists hold that Christ will return before a literal thousand-year kingdom on earth. In it God fulfils his unconditional promises to national Israel: the land, David's throne in Jerusalem, and Israel's blessing among the nations. Most hold that the church is raptured before a seven-year tribulation, Daniel's seventieth week. Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock) say the Davidic kingdom is already inaugurated in Christ, but still expect a future earthly stage.

Revelation is read as mainly future from chapter 4 onward, and chapter 20 follows chapter 19 in strict order. The six mentions of 'a thousand years' are taken in their plain sense. The kingdom fulfils the prophets' picture of a renewed earth under Messiah's reign from Jerusalem.

Future and total. After Christ returns, an angel removes Satan from the earth and seals him in the abyss for a thousand years. Dispensationalists argue that the New Testament shows Satan as very active now: he fills hearts (Acts 5:3), works in the disobedient (Ephesians 2:2), and the whole world lies in his power (1 John 5:19).

The bodily resurrection of the righteous, which happens in stages: Christ the firstfruits, the church at the rapture, then Old Testament saints and tribulation martyrs at the start of the kingdom (Daniel 12:2; Revelation 20:4). All who share in it are 'blessed and holy'. The unbelieving dead are raised after the thousand years for the final judgment.

Literal: one thousand years. The number is given six times in Revelation 20:2-7, and dispensationalists see no signal in the text that it is a figure. A consistent literal, grammatical and historical method of interpretation (Ryrie) leads them to read it as stated.
Rapture of the church
Seven-year tribulation (Daniel's seventieth week)
Return of Christ in glory
Thousand-year kingdom on earth; Christ reigns from Jerusalem
Final rebellion and the great white throne judgment

Dispensationalists expect the church age to end in growing apostasy and moral decline (2 Timothy 3:1-5; 2 Thessalonians 2:3). Yet they stress worldwide evangelism and expect many to be saved, even during the tribulation (Revelation 7:9-14). The line shows the world's general direction, not the church's faithfulness or fruit. The kingdom's universal triumph comes when Christ establishes it at his return.

It offers a consistent literal reading of both the Old Testament promises to Israel and Revelation 20. It explains texts such as Isaiah 65:20 and Zechariah 14:16-19 that show death and disobedience under Messiah's reign. It has fuelled major missionary, Bible-teaching and Bible-college movements.

Critics say the system as a whole arose only in the 1830s with Darby, and that its sharp Israel-church distinction does not fit texts that make Jew and Gentile one new people (Ephesians 2:14-16). Sacrifices in a millennial temple (Ezekiel 40-48) seem to conflict with Hebrews 10:18. Dispensationalists reply that premillennialism itself is ancient, and that the sacrifices are memorials or for ceremonial cleansing, not atonement.
Does Revelation 20 follow chapter 19 in time?

No. Chapter 20 starts a new vision that goes back to the start of the age, as chapter 12 does. The battle in 20:8 uses the same words as 16:14 and 19:19 ('gather them to the war') and draws on Ezekiel 38-39, as 19:17-21 does. So it is one final battle seen twice. Also, if 19:18-21 destroys all the nations, none are left for Satan to deceive in 20:3.

Most modern postmillennialists (Gentry) agree that chapter 20 recapitulates and shows the whole church age from heaven's side. Some older postmillennialists read it as a later stage of the church age, after Christ conquers the beast in chapter 19 by the sword of his mouth (19:15), that is, by his word rather than his bodily return.

Yes. The visions run in order. The beast and false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire in 19:20, and Satan is thrown in later 'where the beast and the false prophet are' (20:10). The binding of Satan completes the defeat of the dragon's allies in chapter 19. Ladd sees this as the natural reading.

Yes, in strict order: return, binding of Satan, kingdom, release, final judgment, new creation. On the 'no nations left' objection, dispensationalists note that 19:21 speaks of the armies gathered against Christ, not every living person. Believing survivors of the tribulation enter the kingdom (Matthew 25:31-34).
Is Satan bound now?

Yes. Jesus uses the same word, 'bind', for his victory over Satan in Matthew 12:29, and he speaks of Satan cast out (John 12:31) and fallen (Luke 10:18). The binding in Revelation 20:3 is limited to one purpose: Satan can no longer deceive the nations. He still attacks believers, but he cannot stop the gospel reaching all peoples.

Yes, and the binding grounds postmillennial hope. Christ disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Because the strong man is bound, his house is being plundered: nation after nation will be freed from his deception through the preaching of the gospel.

No. Revelation 20 describes removal, not restraint: Satan is thrown into the abyss, shut in and sealed. Yet Peter and Paul describe him now as roaming and blinding minds (1 Peter 5:8; 2 Corinthians 4:4). Ladd grants that Satan was truly defeated at the cross, but sees Revelation 20 as a further, future stage.

No. Satan is 'the god of this age' (2 Corinthians 4:4) and the whole world lies in his power (1 John 5:19). Waymeyer argues that Revelation 20:3 means Satan stops deceiving the nations entirely, which is plainly not true today. Matthew 12:29 concerns Jesus's power over demons in his ministry, not the event of Revelation 20.
What is the first resurrection?

A spiritual resurrection. Many amillennialists read it as the believer's soul going to reign with Christ at death, since John sees 'souls' (20:4); Kline argued that it is the natural counterpart to 'the second death'. Others see the new birth. In John 5:25 Jesus speaks of the spiritually dead hearing his voice 'now', before the bodily resurrection of 5:28-29.

Spiritual, with the stress on regeneration and the believer's share in Christ's present reign (Ephesians 2:6). John 5 shows Jesus himself speaking of two resurrections: a spiritual one now and a bodily one at the last hour. Revelation 20 follows the same pattern.

Bodily. The rest of the dead 'came to life' in 20:5 with the same verb, and that is plainly bodily. As Alford argued, a spiritual first and a bodily second in the same passage makes language meaningless. John 5 marks its shift clearly ('now is' versus 'is coming'), while Revelation 20 gives no such signal.

Bodily. The Greek word for resurrection (anastasis) nearly always means bodily resurrection in the New Testament. The first resurrection is a class rather than one moment: all the righteous, raised before the kingdom in stages. The beheaded martyrs 'came to life' in order to reign; souls in heaven are already alive.
Are there two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart?

No. Daniel 12:2, John 5:28-29 and Acts 24:15 all speak of the righteous and the wicked raised together, in one 'hour'. Jesus says believers are raised 'on the last day' (John 6:40), which leaves no later day for a second resurrection. The clearer texts should govern a highly symbolic vision.

No. Postmillennialists agree with amillennialists: one general resurrection at the return, followed at once by the judgment of all (Matthew 25:31-46). Paul places 'the end' at Christ's coming (1 Corinthians 15:23-24).

Yes. Daniel and Jesus name both groups but do not say they rise at the same moment, just as the prophets merged Christ's two comings into one picture. The 'hour' of John 5:25 already spans the whole church age, so the 'hour' of 5:28 can span a long period too. Revelation 20 supplies the detail of the thousand-year gap.

Yes. Jesus speaks of 'the resurrection of the just' (Luke 14:14), and Paul longs to attain the resurrection 'from among the dead' (Philippians 3:11), suggesting believers rise apart from the rest. Some follow S. P. Tregelles in reading Daniel 12:2 as two groups raised at different times, a reading most Hebrew scholars dispute.
Isaiah 65:17-25: is there death in the new heavens and new earth?

Isaiah describes the eternal new creation in terms his hearers could grasp. The line about a hundred-year-old dying young is a poetic way to say death has lost its power: no infant deaths, lives beyond counting. The passage is headed 'new heavens and a new earth' (65:17), which Revelation 21 places after the millennium, so it cannot describe an era of mortals before it.

Gentry and other postmillennialists read Isaiah 65 as the new creation already begun in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17) and growing more visible as the gospel prevails. Long life with lingering death fits a world being transformed but not yet perfected: the later golden age before the return.

Death and sinners (65:20) cannot belong to the eternal state, where death is no more (Revelation 21:4). So Isaiah describes a stage before final perfection, the millennium, which brings the new creation's blessings in part. Like other prophets, Isaiah blends near and final stages into one picture.

A key millennial text. Mortals live in Messiah's kingdom with very long lives, building houses and planting vineyards. Death still occurs, so this is neither heaven nor the eternal state. Isaiah 'telescopes' the kingdom and the new creation that follows it, a pattern dispensationalists call prophetic foreshortening.
1 Corinthians 15:23-28: is there an interval after 'then comes the end'?

No. 'Then comes the end' follows Christ's coming directly. Death, the last enemy, is destroyed when believers rise at his coming (15:54-55). So no age of ongoing death can come after the return. Christ's reign 'until' all enemies are subdued (15:25) is his present reign from heaven.

No, and this is a central postmillennial text. Christ reigns now 'until' all enemies are under his feet (Psalms 110:1), and only death is left at the last. So his enemies are progressively subdued in history before he returns, and his return defeats the last enemy, death. Gentry argues this leaves no room for a later earthly millennium.

Yes. Paul gives an order: Christ the firstfruits, 'then' those who are Christ's at his coming, 'then' the end. There has already been a gap of two thousand years between the first two stages. The word for 'then' (eita) can mark another interval, so a reign between his coming and the end fits Paul's pattern. Ladd and Blomberg see the millennium hinted at here.

Yes. The three stages allow a gap between Christ's coming and 'the end', when he hands the kingdom to the Father after reigning. His reign 'until' his enemies are subdued is the millennial reign on earth, and death is finally destroyed after it (Revelation 20:14).
Does 2 Peter 3 leave room for a millennium?

No. Peter ties together the coming of the Lord, the day of judgment for the ungodly, the burning of the present heavens and earth, and the new heavens and earth (3:7, 10-13). They form one event. There is no room for a thousand-year earthly reign between the return and the new creation.

No. Peter's single 'day of the Lord' brings judgment and new creation together. The delay the scoffers mock is God's patience, so that many will repent (3:9). Postmillennialists see this as fitting a long age of gospel advance before the end. (A few preterist writers apply this chapter to AD 70; most postmillennialists, like Gentry, apply it to the final return.)

Yes. Peter's 'day of the Lord' is a period, not a single day; he himself reminds readers that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years (3:8). The day can begin at Christ's coming and end with the burning of the old order after the millennium. Peter is not giving a full timetable.

Yes. In prophecy the day of the Lord is an extended period. It begins with judgment, includes the kingdom, and ends with the dissolving of the heavens and earth (Revelation 20:11; 21:1). Walvoord and Pentecost place 2 Peter 3:10 at the close of that day, after the millennium.
What did the early church believe about the millennium?

Amillennialists grant that chiliasm, the hope of a future earthly millennium, was common in the second century (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus). But Justin himself admits many true Christians thought otherwise (Dialogue 80). Charles Hill argues that early non-chiliasts held a coherent hope centred on the intermediate state. Augustine, once a chiliast, taught that the millennium is the church age, and this became the dominant view for over a thousand years.

Postmillennialists grant that their view took full shape later, among the Reformers' heirs and the Puritans. They see its roots in Augustine's present-reign reading and in the early church's hope that the nations would turn to Christ. They note that the early creeds confess one return to judge the living and the dead, with no future earthly millennium.

This is a strength of the view. Papias, who is said to have heard John, as well as Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and Lactantius, expected an earthly kingdom after Christ's return. Justin calls it the belief of Christians who are 'right-minded' in all things. Historic premillennialists argue it declined because of Origen's allegorical method and Augustine's influence, not because of better exegesis.

Dispensationalists claim the early chiliasts as forerunners of their premillennialism. They grant that the fathers did not teach a pretribulation rapture or a full Israel-church distinction; whether Pseudo-Ephraem taught a pretribulation rapture is disputed. They see the eclipse of chiliasm after Augustine as a loss of literal interpretation, later recovered in part.
Will the gospel conquer the world before Christ returns?

The gospel will reach all nations, and the kingdom grows from tiny beginnings (Matthew 13:31-33). But the parable of the weeds shows good and evil growing together until the harvest (13:30), and the New Testament expects the church to suffer through the age. So amillennialists expect worldwide spread, not worldwide Christian dominance, before the return.

Yes. The mustard seed becomes the largest plant, and the leaven fills all the dough: the kingdom grows in reach and in depth. Christ sits at God's right hand until his enemies become his footstool (Psalms 110:1), and he has all authority to disciple the nations (Matthew 28:18-19). Postmillennialists expect most of humanity to be converted, by the Spirit through preaching.

The parables show the kingdom's surprising growth from small beginnings, not its total victory before the end. Ladd stresses that the kingdom is present in power but hidden; its open triumph waits for the return. Jesus asks whether he will find faith on earth when he comes (Luke 18:8), and Paul expects a final rebellion (2 Thessalonians 2:3).

No. The gospel will be preached in the whole world as a witness (Matthew 24:14), but the age ends in apostasy and the rule of the Antichrist. Psalms 110:1 is fulfilled when Christ returns and rules; his enemies are subdued by his direct action, not by gradual conversion. Many dispensationalists read the leaven as evil spreading within Christendom, a reading disputed even among them.
Zechariah 14 and the nations' pilgrimage to Jerusalem: millennium or symbol?

Zechariah pictures God's final triumph in the language of Israel's worship. The nations going up to Jerusalem is fulfilled as people from every nation come to the heavenly Jerusalem through the gospel (Hebrews 12:22; Galatians 4:26). The feast and the threat of drought are the prophet's way of saying that all peoples will worship the Lord as King.

Postmillennialists see the pilgrimage of the nations as the great ingathering of the gospel age. From Pentecost onward the nations stream to Zion (Isaiah 2:2-4) as they turn to Christ. The closing verses, where even cooking pots are holy (14:20-21), picture whole societies made holy as the gospel prevails.

Many historic premillennialists see Christ's return in 14:4-5, followed by his reign over the whole earth (14:9), where surviving nations must still be told to worship. Some allow that the details are symbolic, but hold that the order, return and then rule over mortal nations, supports a kingdom between the return and the eternal state.

A literal picture of the millennium. The Lord's feet stand on the Mount of Olives at his return (14:4). Then surviving nations go up each year to Jerusalem to worship the King and keep the Feast of Booths. Punishment for refusing shows that sin and death remain in the kingdom, so this cannot be the eternal state.
Who populates a millennium with mortals?

This is a key objection to premillennialism. At the return believers are changed into immortal bodies (1 Corinthians 15:51-52), and unbelievers face judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:7-10; Revelation 19:21). No mortal people would be left to fill a kingdom or to rebel later, so the rebellion of Gog and Magog (20:8) must come before the return.

Postmillennialists agree that the return brings the judgment of all. In their view the golden age is filled with ordinary mortal people converted by the gospel before the return, so the problem does not arise for them.

Ladd and others answer that Revelation 19:21 refers to the armies gathered against Christ, not every human being. Survivors from the nations who did not join that battle enter the kingdom and are ruled by Christ and his glorified saints (Revelation 2:26-27; 20:4). Some of their descendants are deceived when Satan is released.

Believers who survive the tribulation enter the kingdom in mortal bodies: Israel's believing remnant and believing Gentiles, the 'sheep' of Matthew 25:31-46. They marry and have children. Some descendants obey only outwardly, and they join the final rebellion when Satan is released (Revelation 20:7-9).
Why do the date of Revelation and the reading of the Olivet discourse matter for the millennium debate?

Most amillennialists accept the late date (about AD 95), but read Revelation as portraying the whole church age, so their view does not depend on the date. Many see parts of the Olivet discourse fulfilled in AD 70 and other parts at the final coming. The date of Revelation is disputed.

The date matters a great deal for preterist postmillennialists. If Revelation was written before AD 70 (Gentry), its great tribulation and beast refer to the Jewish War and Nero, and the 'great tribulation' of Matthew 24 is past. The worst predicted woes then lie behind the church, not ahead, which clears the way for an optimistic future. Not all postmillennialists are preterists.
